newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MORNING UPDATE.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN BROADCASTING CORP MORNING UPDATE.

text.p: QUENSLAND COAL STRIKE STILL ON
Striking miners at Central Queensland's Curragh Coal mine say they will remain on the grass and the company will have to bring in contractors if it wants to resume production.
Curragh management has said it will re-start mining as early as next week on the orders of parent company, ARCO Australia.
Union spokesman Hector Heumuller said the workers go into combat mode today.
"It means that the company is directing their management to start digging coal by whatever means is possible," he said.
"Now that could be contract, that could be staff, there's no other way of doing it, because they won't get the permanent work because there's no agreement."
LABOR TO DELIVER IR ALTERNATIVE
The Federal Opposition says it will deliver a different approach to industrial relations, moving away from enterprise bargaining and back to the award system.
Shadow Industrial Relations minister Bob McMullan said Labor's approach will be different from the Coalition's but also different from the approach of the Keating Government.
He said Labor has been listening to Australian workers and they don't want the increased pressure from enterprise bargaining which he said the Government is forcing on them.
Mr McMullan said Labor's alternative will emphasise job security, strengthen the traditional award system and implement industry-wide arrangements to deliver decent wage rises to workers.
RESEARCHERS CLOSE TO HOLY GRAIL'

Scientists working in a British laboratory are claiming to be close to grasping the holy grail of physics, a breakthrough which could solve all the world's energy problems forever. A Japanese team using facilities in Didcot, Oxfordshire, are experimenting with a form of cold fusion to smash the hearts of atoms together, releasing huge amounts of energy.
According to a report in New Scientist Magazine, they are close to the all-important point where the process produces more energy than it uses.
Solving this problem would open up the possibility of a limitless source of cheap, safe energy using as its raw material hydrogen, the most abundant substance in the universe.
RESEARCH SHOWS CHANGE IN SAVING HABITS
New research suggests there has been a big change in where people are putting most of their savings.
The Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research surveyed 1,200 people nationally and found considerable changes in saving habits over the past four years.
In 1993, 77 per cent of people put their money into banks, building societies and credit unions.
But this year only 64 per cent of people are favouring those organisations.
The survey shows that share ownership and managed trusts are now used by one third of people, more than double the figure four years ago.
The survey figures for most other types of saving, such as houses, holiday homes and superannuation have remained fairly static.
HIGH COURT DECISON ON KAKADU MINE EXPECTED TODAY
The High Court is expected to hand down a decision today on whether a mining company's leases in Kakadu National Park are valid.
Newcrest Mining is seeking damages from the Commonwealth.
The Northern Territory Government renewed Newcrest's Coronation Hill leases after the Commonwealth had included the area in Kakadu National Park, where mining is prohibited.
The Commonwealth claims only it had the power to renew such leases.
A full bench of the Federal Court ruled the mining leases were invalid but Newcrest disagreed and took the matter to the High Court.
Newcrest also claims the Commonwealth, by incorporating its leases in Kakadu, deprived the company of its property on other than just terms, therefore breaching the Constitution.
The Territory Government was a party to proceedings and the decision's expected to be handed down this morning.
COSMONAUTS FACE UNCERTAIN WELCOME
After six drama-filled months in space, two Russian Cosmonauts aboard the crippled Space Station Mir, are about to go home.
Although the pair have had to cope with fire, an oxygen system failure and a collision with a supply vessel, their welcome home may not be a warm one.
For Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin the relief at getting off Mir is likely to be tempered by concern over how they will be treated back on Earth.
President Boris Yeltsin has already suggested he holds the crew responsible for the troubles which have plagued the ageing station.
The capsule carrying the two departing cosmonauts is due to undock from Mir this evening and should land in the Central Asian region of Kazakhstan after a three-hour descent.
